guides.content:
# libtmux for Perl
libtmux for Perl is a tmux client library for creating sessions, arranging windows, sending input, and querying captured state with ordinary Perl arrays. Core and workspace use the Perl standard library at runtime; the optional async distribution adds Futures and a caller-owned event loop. [Quick start](#server-new_session-create-a-session-and-arrange-its-windows) · [Filter panes](#selection-where-filter-with-criteria-and-perl-callbacks) · [Packages](#choose-a-package) · [Documentation](https://libtmux.org/en/perl/) · [Guides](https://libtmux.org/en/perl/latest/guides/) · [API reference](https://libtmux.org/en/perl/latest/reference/) · [CPAN](https://metacpan.org/dist/LibTmux) ## [`Server->new_session`][server-new-session]: create a session and arrange its windows Use Perl 5.44 and tmux 3.3a–3.8 on Linux x86_64 LP64, including WSL. With Perl and cpm on `PATH`, install the published core distribution from CPAN: ```console $ cpm install \ --global \ LibTmux ``` Run the [complete program](packages/core/examples/quickstart.pl) with an explicit socket path. It creates a session, splits its editor window, adds a logs window, and retains a snapshot. It removes only the session it created, including on failure; it preserves any other sessions on the selected server. Save the program below as `quickstart.pl`, or run the linked file from a checkout: ```console $ perl quickstart.pl "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/libtmux-perl-$$.sock" ``` ```perl use v5.44; use LibTmux::Server; my $socket = shift @ARGV // die "Usage: $0 SOCKET_PATH [TMUX]\n"; my $server = LibTmux::Server->new( socket_path => $socket, executable => shift(@ARGV) // 'tmux', config_file => '/dev/null', ); my ($session, $snapshot, $failure); try { $session = $server->new_session( name => 'perl-quickstart', command => [$^X, '-e', 'while () { print }'], ); my $editor = $session->window_links->one->window; $server->rename_window(window => $editor, name => 'editor'); $server->split_pane( pane => $editor->panes->one, horizontal => true, command => [$^X, '-e', 'while () { print }'], ); $server->new_window( session => $session, name => 'logs', command => [$^X, '-e', 'while () { print }'], ); $snapshot = $server->snapshot; } catch ($error) { $failure = $error; $session //= $error->created if $error isa LibTmux::X::Creation; } if ($session) { try { $server->kill_session(session => $session) } catch ($cleanup) { warn "session cleanup failed: $cleanup\n"; $failure //= $cleanup; } } die $failure if defined $failure; # The captured graph remains readable after its live session has gone. for my $link ($snapshot->session_by_id($session->id)->window_links->@*) { my $count = $link->window->panes->count; say $link->window->name, ': ', $count, $count == 1 ? ' pane' : ' panes'; } ``` The captured graph remains readable after the live session is removed: ```text editor: 2 panes logs: 1 pane ``` [`Server`](https://libtmux.org/en/perl/latest/reference/libtmux-server/) owns explicit commands. Its [`new_session`](https://libtmux.org/en/perl/latest/reference/libtmux-server-new_session/) starts tmux when the selected socket has no server. Construction alone does no I/O. The example uses an empty tmux configuration and literal Perl command arrays; it needs no editor, shell wrapper, Python, or repository fixture. An existing session with the example's name is a conflict, not a cleanup target. ## [`Selection->where`][selection-where]: filter with criteria and Perl callbacks Continue with the retained `$snapshot` above. A [`Selection`](https://libtmux.org/en/perl/latest/reference/libtmux-selection/) is a blessed array reference: declarative `where`, one-argument `grep`, and ordinary `map` work together without another tmux call. ```perl my $snapshot = $server->snapshot; my $panes = $snapshot->windows->one({name => 'editor'}) ->panes->where({width => {-gte => 1}}) ->grep(sub ($pane) { $pane->height > 0 }); my @ids = map { $_->id } $panes->@*; my $active = $panes->one({active => true}); say 'editor panes: ', scalar @ids; say 'active pane belongs to ', $active->window->name; ``` `one` throws on zero or multiple occurrences. `one_or_undef` represents absence and still rejects ambiguity. `to_array` makes a fresh unblessed arrayref. Native array access stays mutable; library methods validate all members. The [filtering guide](docs/filtering.md) covers nulls, numeric comparisons, same-child quantifiers, and invalid-filter diagnostics. ## [`Server->send_text`][server-send-text]: send text, capture output, and set environment The [live workflow](packages/core/examples/workflow.pl) performs this section while its session is still open: ```perl $server->send_text( pane => $right, text => 'hello from Perl', enter => true ); my $screen = $server->capture_pane(pane => $right, start => -100); say 'captured bytes: ', length $screen; $server->set_environment( session => $session, name => 'PROJECT', value => 'api', ); say 'PROJECT=', $server->get_environment(session => $session, name => 'PROJECT'); ``` [`send_text`](https://libtmux.org/en/perl/latest/reference/libtmux-server-send_text/) sends literal text; `send_keys` accepts tmux key names. [`capture_pane`](https://libtmux.org/en/perl/latest/reference/libtmux-server-capture_pane/) returns current screen/history bytes. Command acceptance does not prove that a pane application finished its work. Use an application-specific observable completion condition when that matters. See [orchestration](docs/orchestration.md). ## [`LibTmux::Filter`][filter]: save a reusable filter [`Filter`](https://libtmux.org/en/perl/latest/reference/libtmux-filter/) compiles criteria once and owns its normalized data. In the same workflow: ```perl my $filter = LibTmux::Filter->new( entity => 'pane', where => {active => true, width => {-gte => 1}}, ); my $restored = LibTmux::Filter->from_json($filter->to_json); my $selected = $panes->where($restored); say 'restored filter matches: ', $selected->count; ``` The `libtmux.where/v1` wire format preserves schema-selected text, numbers, booleans, and nulls. Native `qr//` remains available in callbacks; serialized regex dialects are deferred. [Query plans](docs/query-planning.md) explain which scalar predicates can be verified by tmux. ## Choose a package | Distribution | Use it for | Package and API | | --- | --- | --- | | [LibTmux](packages/core/README.md) | Commands, snapshots, graph navigation, filtering, options and environment. Perl standard library at runtime. | [CPAN](https://metacpan.org/dist/LibTmux) · [API](https://libtmux.org/en/perl/latest/reference/) · [POD](https://metacpan.org/pod/LibTmux) | | [LibTmux-Async](packages/async/README.md) | Concurrent Future-returning operations and explicit executor cleanup. Adds Future, IO::Async, IO::Async::Loop::Ppoll and IO::Ppoll. | [CPAN](https://metacpan.org/dist/LibTmux-Async) · [API](https://libtmux.org/en/perl/latest/reference/libtmux-async-server/) · [POD](https://metacpan.org/pod/LibTmux::Async) | | [LibTmux-Workspace](packages/workspace/README.md) | Validate, plan, and load JSON workspaces with a library or CLI. Uses core and the Perl standard library. | [CPAN](https://metacpan.org/dist/LibTmux-Workspace) · [API](https://libtmux.org/en/perl/latest/workspace/reference/libtmux-workspace/) · [POD](https://metacpan.org/pod/LibTmux::Workspace) | Each package has its own README, license, metadata, and runnable consumer examples. Async closes its executor without destroying a borrowed tmux server. Workspace uses public synchronous core APIs and does not require async. Install either companion by module name; its declared core dependency is installed automatically: ```console $ cpm install \ --global \ LibTmux::Async ``` ```console $ cpm install \ --global \ LibTmux::Workspace ``` The `0.x` API can change between releases. Read each distribution's `Changes` file before upgrading and pin versions in applications that need a fixed API. ## Run the examples and read the guides [The examples index](examples/README.md) separates standalone installed-package programs from repository qualification demos. The runner checks output, cleanup, and preservation of borrowed sessions: ```console $ mise exec -- make examples ``` Read [installation](docs/installation.md), [orchestration](docs/orchestration.md), [filtering](docs/filtering.md), [graph identity](docs/graph.md), [query planning](docs/query-planning.md), [async execution](docs/async.md), [workspace loading](docs/workspace.md), and [errors and recovery](docs/errors.md). Installed API documentation uses POD: `perldoc LibTmux::Server`. [Compatibility](docs/compatibility.md) covers tmux 3.3a–3.8 inclusive; CI tests only Perl 5.44 and the two tmux endpoints. Persistent control, streaming subscriptions, tmux command chaining, serialized regexes, and relation pushdown are deferred. [Architecture decisions](docs/dev/adr/index.md) explain the contracts and costs. [Contributing](.github/CONTRIBUTING.md) covers author setup and checks. [Perl choices](.github/PERL.md) records dependency decisions; [branding](docs/branding.md) describes the logos and social cards. [server-new-session]: https://libtmux.org/en/perl/latest/reference/libtmux-server-new_session/ [selection-where]: https://libtmux.org/en/perl/latest/reference/libtmux-selection-where/ [server-send-text]: https://libtmux.org/en/perl/latest/reference/libtmux-server-send_text/ [filter]: https://libtmux.org/en/perl/latest/reference/libtmux-filter/

---
title: Install Perl packages
description: Install the independent Perl core, async, and workspace distributions.
---

Use Perl 5.44 and tmux 3.3a–3.8 on Linux x86_64 LP64, including WSL. Install
the packages you need from CPAN, or use a source checkout for development.
The [documentation homepage](https://libtmux.org/en/perl/) links the guides
and [API reference](https://libtmux.org/en/perl/latest/reference/).

## Install from CPAN

Install [Perl](https://www.perl.org/get.html) and
[cpm](https://github.com/skaji/cpm#installation), then keep the same interpreter
and installation prefix for all selected packages.

Install [LibTmux](https://metacpan.org/dist/LibTmux) for commands, snapshots,
and filtering:

```console
$ cpm install \
    --global \
    LibTmux
```

Add [LibTmux-Workspace](https://metacpan.org/dist/LibTmux-Workspace) for the
JSON library and packaged `libtmux-workspace` CLI:

```console
$ cpm install \
    --global \
    LibTmux::Workspace
```

Add [LibTmux-Async](https://metacpan.org/dist/LibTmux-Async) for Future-returning
operations:

```console
$ cpm install \
    --global \
    LibTmux::Async
```

The companions declare their core dependency; the installer resolves it
automatically. Core and workspace use the Perl standard library at runtime.
Async adds Future, IO::Async, IO::Async::Loop::Ppoll, and IO::Ppoll; the latter
includes an XS extension and requires a C compiler. Configure and test
dependencies are declared separately and resolved by the installer. Consumer
programs do not require the repository's author tools or Python. Other loop
backends and Linux ABIs are unsupported.

The `0.x` API can change between releases. Consult each distribution's
`Changes` file before upgrading and pin versions in applications that need a
fixed API.

## Prepare a source checkout

Install [Perl](https://www.perl.org/get.html) and
[cpm](https://github.com/skaji/cpm#installation). With mise installed, this
checkout's `.tool-versions` selects Perl 5.44.0. Clone the repository:

```console
$ git clone https://github.com/libtmux/libtmux-perl.git
```

```console
$ cd libtmux-perl
```

If the pinned interpreter is not installed:

```console
$ mise install
```

Check the interpreter selected for installation and execution:

```console
$ mise exec -- perl -v
```

The [contributor setup](../.github/CONTRIBUTING.md#environment) supplies a
hash-verified standalone cpm installer and an isolated author environment.
Consumer programs do not require those author tools or Python. Keep the same
Perl interpreter and installation prefix for all selected distributions.

## Install from the source checkout

With Perl 5.44 and cpm on `PATH`, install core from the repository root:

```console
$ cpm install \
    --global \
    ./packages/core
```

Add workspace for the JSON library and packaged `libtmux-workspace` command:

```console
$ cpm install \
    --global \
    ./packages/workspace
```

Add async for Future-returning operations:

```console
$ cpm install \
    --global \
    ./packages/async
```

## Run a first program

The [core quick start](../packages/core/examples/quickstart.pl) creates its own
session, splits a pane, adds a window, captures the graph, and removes that
session. It starts tmux if the explicit socket is unused:

```console
$ perl packages/core/examples/quickstart.pl "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/libtmux-perl-$$.sock"
```

```text
editor: 2 panes
logs: 1 pane
```

All package examples import installed public modules. No source-tree
`PERL5LIB`, repository fixture, Python, or syscall boilerplate is required.
Use [the examples index](../examples/README.md) to choose filtering, concurrent
operations, workspace loading, or the author qualification programs.

Installed API documentation uses POD:

```console
$ perldoc LibTmux::Server
```

For a missing executable, install tmux or pass its path as the example's second
argument. `NoServer` on `snapshot` means the selected socket has no daemon;
create a session with `new_session` first. A conflicting example session name
is an error and never grants permission to delete that existing session.

---
title: Filter captured selections
description: Native Perl arrays, strict criteria, graph quantifiers, and wire filters.
---

Use `where({...})` for query data and `grep(sub ($pane) {...})` for arbitrary
Perl behavior. Native `->@*`, indexing, `grep`, `map`, `sort`, and List::Util
remain available. `to_array` returns a fresh unblessed array reference.

Fields select comparison semantics: text, safe decimal integers, booleans,
nullability, allowed operators, and relation cardinality come from one catalog.
False, zero, "0", empty text, and undef remain distinct. Integer operands are
bounded to +/-9007199254740991; invalid numeric text never becomes zero.

| Grammar | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| scalar or `-eq`, `-ne` | Schema-directed equality and complement. |
| `-in`, `-not_in` arrays | Explicit membership; empty arrays mean false/true. |
| `-lt`, `-lte`, `-gt`, `-gte` | Authorized numeric ordering. |
| `-contains`, `-starts_with`, `-ends_with` | Literal, case-sensitive text. |
| `-and`, `-or` arrays; `-not` node | Complete criteria nodes. |
| `-some`, `-every`, `-none` | To-many quantifiers over the complete captured domain. |
| `-is`, `-is_not` | To-one criteria or explicit nullable absence. |

Fields/operators in a hash are conjoined. Duplicate Perl hash keys overwrite;
use multiple operators or explicit `-and`. Empty criteria and empty AND are
true; empty OR is false. On a loaded empty relation, some is false and
every/none true. Conditions inside one some apply to the same child; separate
existentials may match different children. Unloaded relations never prove empty.

Full compilation precedes evaluation, even on empty selections. Hash keys
traverse lexically; logical arrays preserve their order. Short-circuiting may
avoid unavailable reads once a result is known. Known-null ordering/text is
false; negation reverses known results, never missing-data failures.

Evaluation order affects failures as well as matches. For an inactive record
with unloaded width, an AND array testing `active` before `width` can return
false; reversing those nodes reads width first and throws. Flattening them into
a hash instead selects lexical order. Wire serialization retains logical-array
order; optimizers must preserve availability and error behavior. The depth-64
and 10,000-node compilation limits do not cap membership operands or string bytes.

Native arrays remain mutable. Every library method validates all N occurrences
before returning even `first`, `count` or `exists`; that validation is O(N).
Predicates may then stop early. `where` evaluates and validates its output;
`iterator` also copies membership. Raw indexing and dereferencing retain normal
Perl behavior. A mutable selection cannot safely cache a prior validation.

`LibTmux::Filter` owns normalized criteria, supports plain records and explicit
registered readers, and exports JSON with schema `"libtmux.where/v1"`.
Wire names use camelCase and dash-free operators. Regex/coderefs/cycles/blessed
values are refused at that data boundary. Native Perl `qr//` remains available
in callbacks.

## Query installed objects and ordinary records

The [live workflow](../packages/core/examples/workflow.pl) creates two editor
panes before running these local queries:

<!-- example: packages/core/examples/workflow.pl#filter -->
```perl
my $snapshot = $server->snapshot;
my $panes =
    $snapshot->windows->one({name => 'editor'})
    ->panes->where({width => {-gte => 1}})
    ->grep(sub ($pane) { $pane->height > 0 });
my @ids    = map { $_->id } $panes->@*;
my $active = $panes->one({active => true});
say 'editor panes: ',          scalar @ids;
say 'active pane belongs to ', $active->window->name;

```

The [record-only program](../packages/core/examples/filters.pl) runs with the
installed core and no tmux server:

```console
$ perl packages/core/examples/filters.pl
```

<!-- example: packages/core/examples/filters.pl#records -->
```perl
my $filter = LibTmux::Filter->new(
    entity => 'pane',
    where  => {
        active          => true,
        current_command => {-in  => [qw(perl vim)]},
        width           => {-gte => 80},
    },
);
my @records = (
    {id => '%1', active => true,  current_command => 'perl', width => 120},
    {id => '%2', active => false, current_command => 'perl', width => 120},
    {id => '%3', active => true,  current_command => 'vim',  width => 40},
);
my @matches = grep { $filter->matches($_) } @records;
say 'matching records: ', join ', ', map { $_->{id} } @matches;

```

It prints `matching records: %1`. Its complete source also checks a JSON
round trip. No author fixture, Python evaluator, or object framework is needed
by either consumer program.

## Save criteria for reuse

In the live workflow, the compiled filter can be stored as versioned JSON and
reused on a captured selection:

<!-- example: packages/core/examples/workflow.pl#wire -->
```perl
my $filter = LibTmux::Filter->new(
    entity => 'pane',
    where  => {active => true, width => {-gte => 1}},
);
my $restored = LibTmux::Filter->from_json($filter->to_json);
my $selected = $panes->where($restored);
say 'restored filter matches: ', $selected->count;

```

Changing the original criteria hash does not change a compiled filter. Schema
validation still applies after decoding; executable callbacks belong in `grep`,
not in the wire data.

## Distinguish one child from two children

One `-some` subtree applies every condition to the same child. Two existential
subtrees can match different children. The workflow limits the domain to its
own editor window and checks both cases:

<!-- example: packages/core/examples/workflow.pl#relations -->
```perl
my $windows    = $snapshot->windows->where({id => $editor->id});
my $same_child = $windows->where(
    {
        panes => {-some => {-and => [{index => 0}, {index => 1}]}},
    }
);
my $different_children = $windows->where(
    {
        -and => [
            {panes => {-some => {index => 0}}},
            {panes => {-some => {index => 1}}},
        ],
    }
);
say 'same child: ',         $same_child->count;
say 'different children: ', $different_children->count;

```

An individual pane cannot have both index 0 and index 1, so `same child` is 0.
The window has both panes, so `different children` is 1. Loaded empty relations
make `-some` false and `-every`/`-none` true. Unloaded relations remain errors
when evaluation needs them. See [graph identity](graph.md).

## Independent-port subset

The shared fixture vocabulary is proposed for this port. A source-pinned Python
QueryList evaluator agrees on the advertised subset: Boolean/integer/text
equality, literal contains/prefix/suffix, membership, and empty membership.
The adaptation maps wire field names to record keys and operators to native
QueryList lookup keywords. It does not claim that Python accepts this wire API.

Known-null equality initially disagreed: the pinned Python filter rejects None
fields before its equality lookup. That difference remains recorded. Numeric
ordering, availability errors, graph quantifiers, validation on empty data,
and canonical-name enforcement have no equivalent declared Python contract
and are marked unsupported, not passed. Perl fixtures cover those semantics.
See [the fixtures](../conformance/where-v1.json) and
[the independent source pin](../scripts/conformance-reference.json).

# Examples

Start with the standalone programs in each native distribution. They use
installed public modules and ordinary Perl; no Python, author fixture, or
source-tree library path is required. The baseline is Perl 5.44 and Linux
x86_64 LP64 with tmux 3.3a–3.8.

## Run an installed-package example

[Install core](../docs/installation.md), then run the quick start from a
checkout with an explicit socket path:

```console
$ perl packages/core/examples/quickstart.pl "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/libtmux-perl-$$.sock"
```

The example starts tmux if necessary, creates and removes its own session,
and preserves other sessions on that socket. Each live program accepts an
optional second argument naming the tmux executable. A conflicting example
session name is an error; existing sessions are never cleanup targets.

| Program | Task | Expected result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Core quick start](../packages/core/examples/quickstart.pl) | Create, split, rename, capture, clean up, and retain the graph. | `editor: 2 panes` and `logs: 1 pane`. |
| [Core workflow](../packages/core/examples/workflow.pl) | Arrange windows, send text, capture output, set environment, filter, compare quantifiers, and verify native queries. | `core workflow: ok`. |
| [Filter records](../packages/core/examples/filters.pl) | Match ordinary hash records, round-trip JSON, and inspect typed validation errors without tmux. | `%1` matches; the invalid numeric operand reports its criterion path. |
| [Async operations](../packages/async/examples/concurrent.pl) | Run concurrent Futures and ordered batches, remove the created session, and await close. | `first` before `second`; `async operations and cleanup: ok`. |
| [Workspace loading](../packages/workspace/examples/load.pl) | Read the adjacent JSON, plan, load, inspect two windows and three panes, repeat with skip, and clean up. | `workspace plan, load, repeat: ok`. |

Async requires the separate distribution and its Ppoll dependencies. Workspace
requires core and the workspace distribution. The packaged JSON uses literal
Perl commands. All examples ship alongside their own distribution's README
and logo assets.

## Run repository qualification programs

The programs in this directory exercise additional contracts through the
repository's fixture. Provision the [author environment](../.github/CONTRIBUTING.md#environment)
first. `Future::AsyncAwait` is needed only for `await.pl`.

```console
$ mise exec -- make examples
```

| Program | Contract |
| --- | --- |
| [quickstart.pl](quickstart.pl) | Select contextual window links, filter captured panes, and verify fixture cleanup. |
| [selection.pl](selection.pl) | Arrays, callbacks, cardinality, wire filters, relations, retained graphs, and native verification. |
| [workspace.pl](workspace.pl) | Plan, load, inspect panes, and repeat with `existing => 'skip'`. |
| [async.pl](async.pl) | Capture through a caller-owned Ppoll loop and await cleanup. |
| [await.pl](await.pl) | Use optional caller-side `async`/`await` syntax with core result objects. |
| [async-lifecycle.pl](async-lifecycle.pl) | Preserve failures, handle cancellation, and observe cleanup without destroying a borrowed server. |

`async-lifecycle.pl` also works with installed packages against an existing
explicit socket. Run its `--help` before using `--fail` or `--cancel`. A
cancelled operation does not prove cleanup has finished; continue driving
the loop until close succeeds.

## How the examples are checked

[The runner](../scripts/run-examples.pl) rejects nonzero exits and missing
expected output. Each live consumer runs with an owned private socket and a
pre-existing sentinel session. After the program exits, the runner verifies
that its session is gone and the borrowed session remains. Fixture teardown
checks process exit and removes owned files.

The tmux endpoint CI cells run the same programs. The installed-artifact job
extracts package examples from the exact native archives, verifies them against
the source, and runs them using only the external installation prefix. No
checkout module path supplies the consumer's imports.

README and guide code blocks marked with `example` come from the complete
program or a named region in it. Check for drift:

```console
$ mise exec -- make check-snippets
```

Keep expected output, source, and documentation consistent. The
[shared capability showcase](https://github.com/libtmux/docs/issues/243)
requires executed examples, recorded CI evidence, and an accurate tmux floor.

---
title: Snapshots and linked-window identity
description: Snapshots and linked-window identity with the Perl libtmux distributions.
---

A physical window can appear at several indexes in one session and in several
sessions. `WindowLink` owns session-relative index and active state. A Pane's
`window` always returns the physical Window. Session changes use explicit links.

Snapshot `windows` and `panes` contain each physical identity once. Raw
`listings` retain contextual rows and multiplicity. Selection filters retain
their own input order and duplicates. Two occurrences of one identity still
make `one` ambiguous.

Selections may combine captures from the same server generation. Each handle
retains its own observed graph; combining them does not reconcile capture times
or create a new snapshot. Mixing server scopes or daemon generations is an
`InvalidSelection` error. Use one snapshot when a query needs one capture interval.
For example, a retained pane captured before a rename and a fresh pane with
the same resource identity can expose different window names. Each traverses
its own graph. Capture start/end metadata describes those observation intervals;
resource identity alone does not identify an observation.

IDs remain strings. Write session IDs as `'$1'` in Perl so regex captures do
not interpolate. Identity includes server, daemon generation, kind, and ID.
Captured handles prevent silent retargeting after a restart; probes and
commands remain separate observations, so they do not form a transaction.
The daemon's `socket_path` identifies the server and `pid/start_time` its
generation. Raw ID strings deliberately target current resources and convey
no historical generation protection.

The store owns scalar records and ID adjacency. Handles strongly retain that
store, which does not strongly own handles. A retained pane keeps its observed
window even when the Snapshot wrapper leaves scope. Retaining one handle can
retain the graph; `to_record` exports detached scalar data instead.
Current to-many accessors scan related records; repeated relation traversal
can repeat that work. Retained-graph memory and indexing improvements require
measurements rather than assumptions about typical tmux graph size.

Acquisition records start/end and completeness. Strict live capture rejects
missing required topology. Unloaded fields and relations throw when needed;
null and loaded-empty relations remain distinct. Accessors return independent
membership arrays. Query methods are nonmutating, while native arrays remain
mutable and every library query validates their members.

## Observe a rename without rewriting history

The [standalone workflow](../packages/core/examples/workflow.pl) retains the
`logs` window from one capture, renames its live counterpart, and checks both
observations:

<!-- example: packages/core/examples/workflow.pl#graph -->
```perl
my $before = $snapshot->window_by_id($logs->id);
$server->rename_window(window => $logs, name => 'build');
die 'captured name changed' unless $before->name eq 'logs';
die 'new name missing'
    unless $server->snapshot->window_by_id($logs->id)->name eq 'build';
say 'captured name: ', $before->name;

```

The old handle still says `logs`; a new capture says `build`. The core quick
start also traverses its retained graph after removing its live session.
Both programs use only installed public modules and explicit sockets.

# Entity fields

Generated from the packaged field catalog. Missing fields throw; known null is explicit.

| Entity | Field | Wire | Type | Nullable | tmux source / minimum |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| client | height | height | integer | no | `client_height` / 3.3a |
| client | id | id | string | no | `client_name` / 3.3a |

---
title: Explicit acquisition and native filters
description: Explicit acquisition and native filters with the Perl libtmux distributions.
---

`$snapshot->panes->where($criteria)` and callbacks evaluate eagerly without
I/O. `query_panes` explicitly acquires a graph and returns a PaneSelection.
`explain_panes` creates a local plan using support-floor capabilities; it does
not connect. Execution binds capabilities to the captured daemon generation.

The [installed-package workflow](../packages/core/examples/workflow.pl)
compares local evaluation and exact native verification on a controlled graph:

<!-- example: packages/core/examples/workflow.pl#query -->
```perl
my $where = {active => true, width => {-gte => 1}};
my $local = $server->query_panes(where => $where, pushdown => 'never');
my $verification;
my $verified = $server->query_panes(
    where           => $where,
    pushdown        => 'require',
    on_verification => sub ($report) { $verification = $report },
);
say 'native verification: ', $verification->{status};

```

`never` still performs acquisition; it disables the extra native candidate
check. The result of either call is a captured local selection. The example
checks identical IDs and observes `native verification: agreed`.

| Policy | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `never` | Acquire and evaluate locally. |
| `auto` | Verify safe scalar native candidates; fall back to captured local results on disagreement. |
| `require` | Require complete exact lowering and native/captured agreement. |

The current implementation captures and evaluates the complete graph before
candidate verification, preserving local error behavior. It makes no I/O-saving
claim. Plans identify commands, lowered filters, residual reasons, and capability
requirements. Numeric lowering uses tmux numeric expressions. Literal operands
are escaped for the tmux grammar independently of argument-vector safety.

`auto` is the default. It costs an extra command and supervisor when lowering
is available. Select `never` when only the captured answer is needed. To inspect
the comparison, supply `on_verification => sub ($report) { ... }`. The observer
receives one detached hashref in void context; its return is ignored. It runs
inline once after a successful decision, including fallback. Exceptions
propagate unchanged unless the operation has already been cancelled;
cancellation suppresses subsequent result/error delivery.
Failed acquisition, decoding or native commands do not
invoke it and remain failures.

The report identifies `status`, `comparison`, capture generation/interval,
executed filter, residual reasons, and captured/local/native ID arrays.
`disabled` means `never`, and `local` means no safe lowering was available.
`agreed` distinguishes exact equality from partial candidate inclusion;
`disagreed` lists missing, unexpected and uncaptured IDs. `native` reports only
captured membership for the expert escape hatch. See
[`Server`'s report contract](../packages/core/lib/LibTmux/Server.pm)
and the [tested query example](../examples/selection.pl).

`require` disagreement throws `LibTmux::X::QueryMismatch`, with the report under
the `verification` key returned by `LibTmux::X::details`. The observer does not
run before that failure.
A mismatch can reflect a race, a compiler defect or a backend difference;
it does not establish which occurred. Matching observations also do not prove
an atomic capture. [ADR 0003](dev/adr/0003-query-verification-diagnostics.md)
records the diagnostic and default-policy decision.

A partial AND conjunct can prune candidates. Partial OR/NOT cannot. Relations,
null, bytes, and unsupported scalar operators remain local. Relation pushdown
and serialized regex dialects are deferred. Complete relation domains are never
pruned before `every` or `none` evaluation.

`native_filter` is an explicit expert escape hatch, exclusive with portable
criteria and pushdown policy. It selects captured root IDs and rejects new IDs
that appeared outside capture. It has native tmux semantics, not wire semantics.

---
title: Recover from failures
description: Recover from failures with the Perl libtmux distributions.
---

Errors are typed `LibTmux::X` objects with readable stringification and
applicable fields such as path, expected/received types, IDs, dispatch state,
and process result. Catch objects with stable Perl try/catch and isa:

```perl
try {
    my $only = $snapshot->panes->one({ active => true });
}
catch ($error) {
    if ($error isa LibTmux::X::NoMatch) {
        say 'No active pane in this captured selection';
    }
    else {
        die $error;
    }
}
```

`one_or_undef` handles absence and still rejects ambiguity. Acquisition errors
never become empty selections. `Unloaded` differs from known null. Complete
criteria validation runs before matching, including on empty input and in
branches that later short-circuit.

Process results distinguish stdout, stderr, exit status, signal, timeout,
spawn failure, output limit, cancellation, and dispatch uncertainty. Lifecycle
errors retain bounded partial results; unknown status remains undef.
Cancellation does not imply rollback or nonexecution. The isolated Linux
supervisor reaps its owned process group; intentionally detached daemons have
separate ownership. The current verified ABI is x86_64 LP64.

Owned supervisor and command branches close unrelated inherited descriptors,
including native descriptors without close-on-exec. The caller's handles stay
open. Only standard streams and the job's explicit protocol/cancellation pipes
survive where needed; a newly started tmux daemon cannot retain an unrelated
caller file or socket. This requires the Linux `/proc/self/fd` interface.
Descriptor enumeration/closure failure prevents dispatch and remains a typed
transport or spawn failure. Forking a host with native threads is unqualified.

Transport `timeout` bounds one command's execution loop, excluding supervisor
setup and async queue waiting. A snapshot runs several commands, each with its
own timeout; this setting is not a total snapshot deadline. Cleanup has a
separate allowance and continues after useful work expires. Async callers must
drive the borrowed loop until successful close-observer completion. Cancelling
the observer or stopping the loop does not prove that processes have exited.

`Creation` preserves a generation-scoped minimal created handle when the
command succeeded but subsequent capture failed. Inspect `created` and `cause`
before deciding cleanup. Other fields on that handle are unloaded. Workspace
uses this evidence for owned rollback and records cleanup failures separately.

## Report an invalid filter without losing its type

The [record-only example](../packages/core/examples/filters.pl) runs without a
tmux server and rejects a text operand for an integer field:

<!-- example: packages/core/examples/filters.pl#invalid -->
```perl
try {
    LibTmux::Filter->new(
        entity => 'pane',
        where  => {width => {-gte => 'wide'}}
    );
    die 'invalid numeric operand was accepted';
}
catch ($error) {
    die $error unless $error isa LibTmux::X::InvalidFilter;
    say 'invalid operand at ', $error->path;
    say 'expected: ',          $error->expected;
}

```

The path is `pane.where.width.-gte`, and `expected` says `safe decimal integer`.
Use the typed [InvalidFilter](https://libtmux.org/en/perl/latest/reference/libtmux-x/)
exception and its fields to choose recovery; stringification is for a readable
diagnostic. Unknown fields and malformed filters fail before examining any
selection members, including on an empty selection.

The [core quick start](../packages/core/examples/quickstart.pl) separately
shows creation receipts and exception-safe session cleanup. The
[async consumer](../packages/async/examples/concurrent.pl) awaits executor
cleanup even after an operation fails. A cleanup failure never replaces the
original operation failure in either example.

---
title: Linux compatibility and qualification
description: Linux compatibility and qualification with the Perl libtmux distributions.
---

The baseline is stable Perl 5.44.0 on Linux x86_64 LP64, including WSL.
Supported tmux versions span 3.3a–3.8, including every intermediate release.
Plain tmux 3.3 is below the 3.3a support floor.
Other operating systems and Linux ABIs have not been qualified. The supervisor
refuses unsupported ABIs before dispatch instead of assuming syscall numbers.

CI and the local compatibility command use only the latest stable Perl and
two tmux releases: the oldest supported release and the newest stable release.
The current pins are [Perl 5.44.0](https://dev.perl.org/perl5/), tmux 3.3a,
and [tmux 3.8](https://github.com/tmux/tmux/releases/tag/3.8), verified on
2026-11-08. Testing the range endpoints keeps CI small; intermediate tmux
releases remain supported without separate CI cells. Older Perl releases
have no matrix cells. Update the pins when the latest stable release changes.

[The source lock](../scripts/tmux-lock.json) pins official assets,
archive hashes, source commits, and configure flags. Per-build provenance adds
compiler and executable hashes. Exact per-cell results are recorded by the
compatibility command; a missing or skipped cell remains unverified.
Earlier wider matrix runs remain historical evidence for their recorded
revisions; they do not add current completion gates.

```console
$ mise exec -- make compatibility
```

The original 3.3a run exposed tmux's invalid-layout error-pointer defect.
The public select_layout wrapper now rejects unknown/ambiguous names lacking
a custom-layout checksum prefix before dispatch. The raw command escape hatch
retains native behavior. See the contributor guide for archive consumers,
examples, units, and the network-free check/provision split.

A local test or build is not hosted CI, a CPAN publication, or a deployed site.
No unrun final-revision gate is implied by these requirements.

---
title: Load a JSON workspace
description: Load a JSON workspace with the Perl libtmux distributions.
---

The separate distribution packages the `libtmux-workspace` CLI. Validate and
plan without tmux I/O; load explicitly through public core APIs.

Save [the packaged configuration](../packages/workspace/examples/workspace.json)
as `workspace.json`, or use that file from the checkout. Its commands are Perl
programs, with two editor panes and a logs window:

<!-- example: packages/workspace/examples/workspace.json -->
```json
{
  "schema": "libtmux.workspace/v1",
  "environment": {"PROJECT": "api"},
  "sessions": [{
    "name": "perl-workspace",
    "windows": [{
      "name": "editor",
      "layout": "even-horizontal",
      "panes": [
        {"command": ["perl", "-e", "while (<STDIN>) { print }"]},
        {"command": ["perl", "-e", "while (<STDIN>) { print }"], "horizontal": true}
      ]
    }, {
      "name": "logs",
      "panes": [{"command": ["perl", "-e", "while (<STDIN>) { print }" ]}]
    }]
  }]
}
```

From the repository root:

```console
$ libtmux-workspace validate packages/workspace/examples/workspace.json
```

```console
$ libtmux-workspace plan packages/workspace/examples/workspace.json
```

```console
$ libtmux-workspace load packages/workspace/examples/workspace.json \
    --socket-path "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/libtmux-perl-workspace-$$.sock" \
    --existing skip
```

Loading leaves the workspace running. The
[standalone Perl example](../packages/workspace/examples/load.pl) additionally
checks the resulting graph, repeats with `skip`, and removes its own session:

```console
$ perl packages/workspace/examples/load.pl "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/libtmux-perl-workspace-$$.sock"
```

Its plan is local and performs no tmux I/O:

<!-- example: packages/workspace/examples/load.pl#plan -->
```perl
open my $in, '<:raw', "$FindBin::Bin/workspace.json" or die $!;
my $json = do { local $/; <$in> };
close $in or die $!;
my $workspace = LibTmux::Workspace->from_json($json);
my $plan      = $workspace->plan;
say 'planned sessions: ', scalar $plan->{sessions}->@*;
die 'plan must not mutate' if $plan->{mutates};

```

It then loads and inspects captured public core objects:

<!-- example: packages/workspace/examples/load.pl#load -->
```perl
my $report   = $workspace->load(server => $server);
my $snapshot = $server->snapshot;
$session = $snapshot->sessions->one({name => 'perl-workspace'});
my $windows = $session->window_links;
say 'loaded windows: ', $windows->count;
my $editor = $windows->one({window => {-is => {name => 'editor'}}})->window;
say 'editor panes: ', $editor->panes->count;

```

Repeating with `skip` preserves the whole existing session:

<!-- example: packages/workspace/examples/load.pl#repeat -->
```perl
my $again = $workspace->load(server => $server, existing => 'skip');
say 'skipped existing sessions: ', scalar $again->{skipped}->@*;

```

The complete program imports installed modules and reads its adjacent JSON;
it needs no author helper. Its output confirms one planned session, two loaded
windows, two editor panes, and one skipped session.

`--dry-run` selects a nonmutating plan. Default `existing=error` checks all
session-name conflicts before creation. `skip` preserves the entire existing
session; repeated loads create only absent sessions. This is not convergence
or reconciliation of an existing layout.

Each pane requires literal `command` argv or explicit `shell_command`.
Environment inherits workspace → session → window → pane; cwd inherits from
window unless overridden. Layout applies after splitting. Configuration is
versioned JSON; no YAML adapter is selected.

On failure, inspect completed steps, failed step, created IDs, dispatch
uncertainty, and cleanup errors. Rollback targets only sessions proven created
by this invocation. Application readiness requires caller-specific assertions.
CLI exit statuses: success 0; usage/configuration 2; loading 3; conflict 4.

`LibTmux::Workspace::X::Load->report` retains each cleanup exception with its
captured target identity and attempted action. These entries replace the
earlier string-only `cleanup_errors` values. `cause` remains the original load
failure; a cleanup failure never replaces it. Catch and inspect the exception
class, dispatch evidence, and bounded native result when choosing recovery.

`report_data` returns a detached diagnostic export for JSON, including the
primary cause and cleanup error classes. Native stdout/stderr use explicit
base64 fields to preserve arbitrary octets. The CLI prints this export on
standard error; the library report keeps the original exception objects.
